doc.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: His place as a conservative player, his father, and teaching at UNO
summary: Brunious feels under-respected as a conservative trumpeter; mentions his father's bands and his teaching at the University of New Orleans.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: This makes a case for jazz education going beyond the classroom, into what we call etiquette. Concert etiquette. But I want to say this about yourself, and then talk a little bit. I see you as being an important person, being a relatively young man, from New Orleans, restoring some of the respect of the music and the tradition. Do you see — where do you see yourself?

Well I don’t feel I am respected enough. Like I don’t think people look at me as real important. I really don’t. Because I don’t know, I’m not one of these real ultra contemporary neo jazz guys. You know what I mean? I’m very much a pretty conservative musician. You know my dad always was a great musician, wrote for Billy Eckstine, Cab Calloway, Jay McShann, Walter Fats Pichon, and all these real bands. You know? And he just taught us to do what was right. Just follow your heart. Do what’s right man. And a lot of times that gets, you know, not recognized in the world as we know it

now. I teach at the University of New Orleans. And the response I get from a lot of these kids is like, oh yeah, well you’re playing old time, or something like that. I mean I’m pretty much a New Orleans and kind of more like a Bebop trumpet player. Which I mean Bebop had the feeling, you know still had the feeling. With all of these modes like Dan was explaining, man, you know I don’t feel that. You know it’s very, very like intellectual. Really like, wow man, that guy must really know some really high-powered stuff, you know, and all of this stuff that comes from Vienna and all of this kind of stuff. You understand what I’m saying. Not to put that down, but I think jazz is like heartfelt. You know that’s art from the heart, not from the brain. But this wave that’s happened, it’s so big we can’t do anything about it. So that’s why I say I don’t feel like really respected or important in that way. Because those kids that I teach and that I encounter all around the country, especially in America, their first thing is I want to be famous. And like is that why you’re playing the horn to be famous man? Don’t you have something to say?
